title: Docker Performance
subtitle: Measure, limit and optimise containers and builds
description: Performance work starts with measurement. Learn how CPU, memory, I/O and build time behave under Docker and where the real bottlenecks are.
outcomes: Apply resource limits without starving services
Reduce image size and startup time

lessons.title: CPU, memory and I/O limits
lessons.summary: What the flags actually do, and why limits without requests can hurt.
objectives: Avoid OOM kills and CPU throttling surprises
Set PID limits against fork bombs

sections.title: Limits are ceilings, not reservations
sections.body:
`--cpus 1.5` sets a CPU quota (150% of one core). `--memory 512m` is a hard limit; exceeding it triggers the OOM killer. `--pids-limit` caps processes and threads. `--blkio-weight` is a relative share, not a bandwidth guarantee.

A container with a CPU quota that is too low will be throttled even when the host is idle. Watch `cpu.stat` (nr_throttled, throttled_time) when latency is unexplained.

sections.code:
docker run -d --name api \
  --cpus 1.5 \
  --memory 512m --memory-swap 512m \
  --pids-limit 256 \
  --blkio-weight 500 \
  acme/api:1.4

docker stats --no-stream
docker inspect api --format '{{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}} {{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.PidsLimit}}'

sections.title: Java and Node need heap awareness
sections.body: A JVM may see host memory unless you set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage or use container-aware defaults. Node’s default heap can also exceed a small container limit.

exercises.title: Set limits
exercises.prompt: Run nginx with 1 CPU and 256 MB hard memory.

exercises.title: Read throttling
exercises.prompt: Find the cgroup for a container and read cpu.stat.
exercises.expected: Use the container id under /sys/fs/cgroup and inspect nr_throttled/throttled_usec.

questions.question: What does --cpus 0.5 mean?
questions.explain: It sets a quota equal to half a core.

questions.question: A container exceeds --memory. What happens?
options: The kernel OOM killer may terminate processes

questions.question: What does --pids-limit protect against?
questions.explain: It caps the number of processes/threads.

lessons.title: Image size and startup
lessons.summary: Smaller images pull faster, start faster and have a smaller attack surface — but size is not the only goal.
objectives: Measure image size and layer contribution
Reduce startup time without breaking signals

sections.title: Where size comes from
sections.body:
Most oversized images contain build tools, package caches, documentation or duplicate dependencies. Multi-stage builds and cache mounts remove build-time bytes. `docker image history` shows which instruction contributed which layer; `dive` gives a file-level view.

Do not chase the smallest possible image blindly. A distroless image is harder to debug; Alpine uses musl, which can break native modules. Optimise for the operational model you can support.

sections.code:
docker image ls --format 'table {{.Repository}}\t{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}'
docker image history --no-trunc acme/api:1.4
docker run --rm acme/api:1.4 du -sh /app /usr/local/lib/node_modules 2>/dev/null

# Compare a shell-form vs exec-form startup
docker inspect acme/api:1.4 --format '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}} {{json .Config.Cmd}}'
sections.note: A smaller image is not automatically faster at runtime; startup is dominated by process initialisation and health checks.

sections.title: Measure pull time in your network
sections.body: A 1 GB image is painful on a slow link even if it is fine in a datacenter. Optimise for the slowest environment that must run it.

exercises.title: Layer audit
exercises.prompt: Find the largest layer in an image.
exercises.expected: docker image history --no-trunc IMAGE and compare sizes.

exercises.title: Measure startup
exercises.prompt: Time a container from start to healthy.
exercises.expected: Use time docker run with a health check, or inspect StartedAt and health status.

questions.question: Which command shows per-layer size contribution?
questions.explain: History lists layer sizes and commands.

questions.question: What is a trade-off of distroless images?
options: They lack a shell and debugging tools
questions.explain: Debugging requires ephemeral containers or a debug variant.

questions.question: Why can Alpine break Node native modules?
options: It uses musl instead of glibc
questions.explain: Prebuilt native binaries may target glibc.

lessons.title: Runtime performance and stats
lessons.summary: Read docker stats correctly, distinguish host and container load, and find the real bottleneck.
objectives: Interpret CPU %, memory usage and I/O counters
Use cgroup data when stats is not enough

sections.title: What docker stats reports
sections.body: CPU % is relative to one core on most platforms, so 250% means 2.5 cores. Memory usage includes page cache for the cgroup; it is not the same as application heap. Network and block I/O are cumulative counters, so compare deltas over time rather than absolute values.

sections.code:
docker stats --no-stream --format 'table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}\t{{.NetIO}}\t{{.BlockIO}}\t{{.PIDs}}'

# Host-level view of a container cgroup
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope/memory.current
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope/cpu.stat

# Process tree
docker top CONTAINER
sections.output:
NAME   CPU %   MEM USAGE / LIMIT   NET I/O         BLOCK I/O     PIDS
api    0.42%   82.1MiB / 512MiB    1.2MB / 840kB   0B / 4.1kB   7

sections.title: A container is not a VM
sections.body: Host CPU steal, memory pressure and disk I/O affect every container. If all containers are slow, look at the host before tuning individual limits.

exercises.title: Baseline
exercises.prompt: Capture three stats samples 5 seconds apart for one container.
exercises.expected: Run docker stats --no-stream repeatedly and compare counters.

exercises.title: Cgroup memory
exercises.expected: Use the cgroup path from docker inspect or systemd-cgls.

questions.question: CPU 250% in docker stats means…
questions.explain: Percent is relative to a single core.
